item.title: Building a tiny weather station!
item.description:
Personal weather station

Recently, I have been more and more passionated about electronics and small hardwares. I decided to slowly build my personal weather station. This is a great Canadian winter hobby and plan to take my time to add more and more measurements.

I started with a small Arduino DHT11 sensor, which measures temperature and relative humidity. It currently is in my home office with a led and an LCD screen. I recently purchased a raspberry pi to anticipate upgrades. Find some real-time plot in the Hobbies section.

item.title: First paper got published!
item.description:
I am pleased to announce that my first article titled “Strengthening Atmospheric Greenhouse Effect at the Arctic North Slope of Alaska Site Evidenced by Long-Term Records of the Downwelling Longwave Radiance Spectrum” has been published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres.

This project analyzed a long-term record of Downwelling Longwave Radiation—the infrared radiation emitted back by the atmosphere (i.e., the greenhouse effect)—at an Arctic site, and compared it to mid-latitude observations where warming is less pronounced.

item.title: What do you mean, "Radiation"?
item.description:
What I’m actually studying (and why it matters)

When people ask me what I’m researching during my Ph.D, they usually expect a simple answer. But like most scientists, my work is pretty specialized! So let me break down what “atmospheric radiation” actually means and why it’s important for understanding climate change.

Heat from Earth: The Invisible Energy We Can’t See

Think of Earth as a giant heater that’s constantly giving off energy. Just like how you feel warmth radiating from a campfire, our planet radiates energy too—but most of it is infrared radiation (heat energy that our eyes can’t see).
